explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Jacob looks up, sees Esau coming with four hundred men, and divides the children among Leah, Rachel and the two maidservants (Genesis 33:1). Leah and Rachel are Jacob's wives. The text shows him sorting the children and doesn't say why. I can't even sort a cookie box without a mess, so I'm impressed.

Close, but the servants aren't what he divides. The text says Jacob divides the children among Leah, Rachel and the two maidservants (Genesis 33:1). The maidservants are in the lineup, but they're part of the groups, not the thing being split. Kids first, friend.

The herds aren't what he divides here. Jacob had already picked out animals to send ahead as a gift (Genesis 32:13-21). In this verse, he divides the children among Leah, Rachel and the two maidservants (Genesis 33:1). Leah and Rachel are his wives. Count heads, not cattle, friend.

Yes, Rachel, Jacob's wife. She and her son Joseph are at the rear (Genesis 33:2). The maidservants and their children go in front, and Leah and her children come next. The text doesn't say why Jacob lined them up this way, so I'll leave that one alone.

Leah is in the lineup, friend, just not at the rear. The text puts the maidservants and their children in front, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear (Genesis 33:2). Leah is Jacob's wife (Genesis 29:23, 25), and she's in the middle spot. The very back belongs to Rachel and Joseph.

Zilpah is Leah's maidservant from earlier in Jacob's story (Genesis 30:9), but this passage doesn't name the maidservants. It only says the maidservants and their children go in front, with Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear (Genesis 33:2). With so many people in this lineup, it's easy to lose track, baker. Rachel is the one at the back.
That's it. Jacob himself goes on ahead of his whole family (Genesis 33:3). Four hundred men are walking up, and he's the first one they'll meet. That takes nerve, and I think it took every bit of it.

Hiding in the back would be tempting, I'll admit it. But the text says Jacob himself went on ahead, and Rachel and Joseph were the ones at the rear (Genesis 33:2-3). He walked toward his brother first. Not one step toward the back, friend.

explanations.answer: Off to the side with his servants
explanations.explanation: Stepping off to the side is how a man avoids the whole thing. Jacob did the opposite. He went on ahead and bowed to the ground seven times as he approached his brother (Genesis 33:3). He walked right up front, where Esau would see him first.

True, baker. Esau ran to him, embraced him, threw his arms around his neck and kissed him (Genesis 33:4). Jacob had bowed to the ground seven times as he approached (Genesis 33:3), and Esau ran to him anyway. I did NOT have that on my bingo card.

It's true, and I know it's hard to believe. The text says Esau ran to Jacob and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept (Genesis 33:4). Jacob had every reason to brace for the worst, and I think that's why this lands so hard.

explanations.answer: God graciously gave them to him
explanations.explanation: Right on. Jacob tells Esau, "These are the children God has graciously given your servant." (Genesis 33:5). He doesn't brag about them. He points to God's grace. And notice he calls himself Esau's servant.

explanations.answer: God gave them as a reward for his work
explanations.explanation: Jacob did work hard for Laban, his father-in-law (Genesis 31:38-41), but that's not what he says here. He says, "These are the children God has graciously given your servant." (Genesis 33:5). Graciously means a gift, not a paycheck. Jacob keeps the credit with God.

explanations.answer: God sent them to make peace with Esau
explanations.explanation: That's a nice thought, but Jacob never says it. He tells Esau, "These are the children God has graciously given your servant." (Genesis 33:5). The text gives no peace-making job for them. It just says they were given by God's grace.

explanations.answer: To find favor in your sight
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jacob says, "To find favor in your sight, my lord…" (Genesis 33:8). Esau came with four hundred men, and Jacob calls him "my lord" and asks for his favor. I've handed over a warm cookie to win somebody over, but this is a whole company. I think it's a humble way to walk up to his brother.

explanations.answer: To repay the debt I owe you
explanations.explanation: Jacob never mentions a debt. When Esau asks about the company, Jacob answers, "To find favor in your sight, my lord…" (Genesis 33:8). He wants his brother's favor, not to settle accounts. No ledger comes out in this scene.

explanations.answer: To show the riches in my hand
explanations.explanation: Jacob doesn't say anything about showing riches. His answer is, "To find favor in your sight, my lord…" (Genesis 33:8). That's the purpose he gives, and it's all about Esau's favor. Showing off a full tray of cookies is more my speed, honestly.
Not quite, baker. Esau says, "I already have plenty, my brother. Keep what belongs to you" (Genesis 33:9). He turns the gift down first. Jacob has to push before it's accepted (Genesis 33:11).

Right, it's false. Esau says, "I already have plenty, my brother. Keep what belongs to you" (Genesis 33:9). Jacob has to press him before he finally accepts (Genesis 33:11). Two brothers, each insisting the other keep the goods. That's a polite standoff, friend.

True, baker. Jacob says, "…I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God, since you have received me favorably." (Genesis 33:10). The reason is in his own words: Esau received him favorably. Earlier, Jacob was greatly afraid when he heard Esau was coming with four hundred men (Genesis 32:6-7). I think that's why this welcome lands so hard.

It's true. Jacob says, "…I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God, since you have received me favorably." (Genesis 33:10). The "since" gives the reason in his own words. Esau's welcome is what he points to.

explanations.answer: His children are frail and his herds are nursing
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jacob says the children are frail and he must care for sheep and cattle that are nursing their young. He adds that if they are driven hard for even a day, all the animals will die (Genesis 33:13). That's the reason he gives for asking Esau to go ahead. A good dad knows his crew's speed.

explanations.answer: His servants are worn out from the long trip
explanations.explanation: The servants aren't his reason. Jacob points to the children being frail and the sheep and cattle nursing their young (Genesis 33:13). The text says nothing about tired servants. The little ones set the pace.

explanations.answer: His wives need to rest for a few days first
explanations.explanation: Jacob never brings up his wives resting, and he never mentions a few days. What he says is that the children are frail and the animals are nursing their young, and a hard drive for even a day would be too much (Genesis 33:13). The pace is for the little ones, baker.

Seir it is. Jacob says he'll come along slowly "…until I come to my lord at Seir." (Genesis 33:14). Seir is the place Esau heads back to (Genesis 33:16). Jacob's promise sounds friendly, and the text then shows him going to Succoth (Genesis 33:17).

Bethel is a real place in Jacob's story (Genesis 28:19), but it's not what he says here. He tells Esau he'll come "…until I come to my lord at Seir." (Genesis 33:14). Seir is where Esau goes next (Genesis 33:16).

Hebron is a real place in the land of Canaan (Genesis 23:2), but it's not what Jacob names here. He says he'll continue slowly "…until I come to my lord at Seir." (Genesis 33:14). Seir is where Esau starts back to that same day (Genesis 33:16). Mixing up place names is easy, friend.

Not this time, baker. Esau offers to leave some of his people, but Jacob replies, "Why do that? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord." (Genesis 33:15). He politely says no. Esau's offer is a kind one, and Jacob still turns it down.

Right. Esau says, "Let me leave some of my people with you…" and Jacob answers, "Why do that? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord." (Genesis 33:15). He doesn't take the offer. Esau leaves for Seir that same day (Genesis 33:16).

Yes, a house, baker. At Succoth, Jacob built a house for himself and shelters for his livestock, and that is why the place was called Succoth (Genesis 33:17). I spent years behind a pile of old takeout menus in a junk drawer, so a roof and four walls sound pretty fancy to me.
A tower is a bold guess, baker. At Succoth, Jacob built a house for himself and shelters for his livestock (Genesis 33:17). No tower anywhere in that verse. We're keeping things low to the ground.

A city wall isn't in the text. At Succoth, Jacob built a house for himself and shelters for his livestock (Genesis 33:17). The verse gives a house and some shelters, and no wall. Good guess on something sturdy, friend.

Succoth is right. Jacob built shelters for his livestock there, "that is why the place was called Succoth." (Genesis 33:17). The name comes from what he built. A whole place named after livestock shelters, baker.

Shechem is a city Jacob reaches after Succoth, where he camps just outside it (Genesis 33:17-18). It's not the place named for the livestock shelters, though. That name is Succoth (Genesis 33:17). Right area, next stop on the map, friend.
Peniel is a place Jacob named earlier, in Genesis 32:30. The place named because of his livestock shelters is Succoth (Genesis 33:17). Peniel is behind him by this point in the story, baker.

True, baker. Jacob camps just outside Shechem, and the plot where he pitched his tent he purchased from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father (Genesis 33:18-19). He paid a hundred pieces of silver for it (Genesis 33:19). He didn't just park and hope. He paid for his spot.

It's true, and it's easy to second-guess. Jacob camped just outside the city (Genesis 33:18). The plot where he pitched his tent, he purchased from the sons of Hamor for a hundred pieces of silver (Genesis 33:19). Hamor's sons sold it, and Jacob paid.
An altar, yes. There Jacob set up an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel (Genesis 33:20). He buys the land, then sets up an altar on it. I think that tells you what mattered to him.
Jacob did set up a stone pillar once, at Bethel (Genesis 28:18). Here the text says he set up an altar (Genesis 33:20). Different place, different thing.

No gate shows up in this passage. On the plot he bought, the text says Jacob set up an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel (Genesis 33:20). A gate isn't mentioned in the verse, so the altar is our answer, friend.
